extracted.intended_audience: journalism students, media studies researchers, and practicing journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and documenting bias in television news broadcasts using systematic, empirical content-analytic and audience-research methods (e.g., videotaped archives, coding of airtime, visual/contextual analysis, and focus groups).

rubrics_metrics.name: Commitment to empirical evidence over theory
rubrics_metrics.description: The project prioritizes meticulous empirical research rather than theory alone, using data to demonstrate bias rather than rely on abstract argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build and analyze concrete data (e.g., videotaped recordings) rather than relying on intuition or purely theoretical claims. Emphasize measurable findings and report them transparently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of video recording and a systematically coded archive
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the then-new technology of video recording to build a systematically coded archive of actual broadcast content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record broadcasts and maintain a searchable videotaped database. Code items consistently so others can re-check analyses; the videotaped archive supports reproducibility and long-term comparative work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic content analysis (who, context, language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze broadcasts by coding who was given airtime, in what context, and with what kind of language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly record speaker identity, segment context, setting, and lexical choices. Quantify representation (e.g., proportions of voices) and report counts/percentages for transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative sampling (primetime and cross-broadcaster comparison)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyse extensive hours of primetime news bulletins across major broadcasters (e.g., BBC and ITN) to identify patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample across comparable time slots and multiple broadcasters to allow cross-comparison; avoid single-source or idiosyncratic samples. Document selection criteria and sampling frame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measuring balance of perspectives (representation metrics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure whose perspectives dominate coverage (e.g., management vs. union voices) and quantify dominance (the GMG found management perspectives dominated in over 80% of segments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report numerical shares of airtime/appearances by actor type; use clear categories (government, corporate, union, workers, community) and present comparative statistics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis of visual context and setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine the visual context in which people are interviewed (e.g., workers on noisy picket lines vs. managers in controlled professional settings) because visuals communicate credibility and authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code and analyze mise-en-scène, location, camera angles, and visual contrast as part of credibility assessment. Consider how setting predisposes viewers to see some sources as authoritative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lexical framing and language choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze language choices that frame actors and actions (for example, describing unions as making “demands” while employers are making “offers”; framing strikes as disruptions rather than responses to grievances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code specific lexical frames and metaphors; track asymmetries (problem-focused vs cause-focused language). Report examples and frequencies of particular terms or frames.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inferential framework / framing analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the inferential frameworks used by news (the news embodies perspectives that make sense of events in preference to other available frameworks — e.g., strikes framed as 'problems' rather than symptoms of inequality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map alternative plausible frameworks and demonstrate which framework(s) the coverage privileges via story selection, story leads, voice prioritization, and imagery. Show how framework choice affects interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hierarchy of credibility and sourcing practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate who is treated as a 'reliable' or authoritative source (government press officers, corporate spokespeople, institutional experts) versus who is marginalized (shop stewards, ordinary workers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code source types, ease of access, and frequency; assess newsroom routines that privilege easy-to-reach authoritative sources. Examine editorial sourcing policies and their practical effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural explanation of bias (routines, socialization, not conspiracy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attribute bias to structural features of journalism (tight deadlines, routines, socialization, dominant ideology) rather than to individual malice or coordinated conspiracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate newsroom workflows, training, background of journalists, and institutional constraints. Use interviews or ethnographic data where possible to document routine behaviors that produce skew.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological transparency and testing of coding schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure coding schemes are explicit and tested for alternatives; critics warned against coding schemes that predefined frames favoring authority without adequate testing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publish coding manuals, inter-coder reliability measures, and tests of alternative coding frames. Guard against circularity and demonstrate that results are robust to reasonable coding variations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of cherry-picking and demonstration of robustness
rubrics_metrics.description: Address the criticism that analyses can be accused of cherry-picking data or imposing political assumptions; ensure selection and interpretation are defensible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pre-specified sampling and coding protocols, conduct sensitivity analyses, and report disconfirming cases. Make raw counts and examples available to allow independent audit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience impact assessment via focus groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Study audiences (e.g., focus groups in Seeing and Believing) to show how television framing shapes viewers' recollections and understandings of events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare interpretations of viewers who rely primarily on TV news with those who have direct connections to events; use qualitative and comparative measures to show how media frames influence beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Longitudinal and cross-topic comparative approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the same empirical approach across topics and decades (industrial disputes, wars, political conflict) to test whether structural patterns persist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect long-term data, apply consistent methods across topics, and compare findings over time and across issue areas to establish generality of patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attention to visual and production practices (beyond text)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include production features (visual context, editing, who is shown and how) as a substantive part of bias analysis, not just spoken words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code editing choices, shot selection, sequence ordering, and use of archival/stock visuals. Consider how production conventions contribute to inferential frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy and institutional implications (sourcing, editorial language, impartiality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider how findings should inform newsroom policies (sourcing policies, editorial language, definitions of impartiality) and how institutions might change practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate empirical findings into concrete policy recommendations (e.g., broaden sourcing, review editorial wording). Document any documented institutional responses or lack thereof.
